title: The Chomsky Hierarchy
summary: Four nested levels of grammar and language complexity — regular, context-free, context-sensitive, and unrestricted — that organize everything the rest of this discipline develops in real depth for the first two.

title: Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA)
summary: A machine with a finite set of states, no memory beyond which state it's in, and exactly one transition per symbol — the simplest formal model of computation, and the one that recognizes exactly the regular languages.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Regular Expressions: Syntax and Semantics
summary: A compact notation for describing a language directly, built from single symbols, concatenation, union, and repetition — the same expressive power as a DFA, in a form that reads like a pattern instead of a machine.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Nondeterministic Finite Automata (NFA)
summary: A machine allowed to have several transitions for the same symbol at once, or none at all — accepting when SOME choice of path leads to acceptance, a looser rule that turns out not to add any real power.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: DFA-NFA Equivalence: The Subset Construction
summary: Every NFA, however tangled its nondeterminism looks, can be converted into an equivalent DFA by tracking every state the NFA COULD be in at once as a single new state — a genuinely surprising result, proved here in full.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Regular Language Closure Properties
summary: Combining two regular languages with union, concatenation, or Kleene star always produces another regular language — a set of guarantees that make it possible to build a complex regular language out of simple, already-known-regular pieces.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: From Regular Expressions to Finite Automata
summary: Building an NFA for a regular expression piece by piece, mirroring its structure exactly — the constructive, straightforward half of Kleene's theorem, proving every regex has an equivalent automaton.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: The Pumping Lemma for Regular Languages
summary: Every regular language has a length past which any long enough string must contain a repeatable middle section — a precise, provable structural fact whose contrapositive is the standard tool for proving a language is NOT regular.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: From Finite Automata to Regular Expressions
summary: The harder direction of Kleene's theorem — eliminating a DFA's states one at a time, building up a regular expression that captures the same language, until only the expression itself remains.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Context-Free Grammars and Derivations
summary: A set of production rules — some referencing themselves, exactly the self-referential shape already familiar from recursion — that generate every string in a language one substitution at a time.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Ambiguity in Grammars
summary: A grammar is ambiguous when some string it generates has more than one valid derivation tree — a real, practical problem for anything built on a grammar, from a calculator's operator precedence to a compiler's parser.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Chomsky Normal Form
summary: Every context-free grammar can be rewritten into one where every rule has exactly one of two fixed shapes — a standardized form that makes later proofs and parsing algorithms possible without losing any generating power.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Pushdown Automata
summary: An NFA given exactly one extra resource — a single stack — which is precisely enough additional memory to recognize every context-free language, and not one language more.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: PDA-CFG Equivalence
summary: Pushdown automata and context-free grammars recognize exactly the same class of languages — two very different-looking formalisms, one procedural and one generative, that turn out to be two views of the same thing.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: The Pumping Lemma for Context-Free Languages
summary: The same pumping idea, one level up the Chomsky hierarchy — a long enough string in a context-free language must have two repeatable pieces, pumped together, giving a standard tool for proving a language is not even context-free.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: Real Applications: Regex in Text Processing, Grammars in Parsers
summary: Two everyday, extremely well-known payoffs of everything covered so far — search-and-replace tools running compiled regular expressions, and a programming language's own syntax defined and parsed by a context-free grammar.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.

title: From Automata to General Computation

related.label: The Church-Turing Thesis and What "Computable" Means

summary: Every model covered here — DFA, NFA, PDA — is fundamentally limited: a fixed amount of memory, or memory shaped only like a single stack. The next discipline removes that limit entirely with the Turing machine.

references.label: Sipser — Introduction to the Theory of Computation, 3rd ed.
